content: Toxicity monitoring has become an essential aspect of treatment and prevention programs, particularly for pregnant and breastfeeding women. Adverse reactions associated with antiretroviral (ARV) drugs are among the most frequently reported reasons for non-adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART), discontinuation of treatment, or substitution of medications. The World Health Organization (WHO) advises countries to adopt a standardized approach to incorporate toxicity monitoring into national monitoring and evaluation (M&E) systems. This approach includes defining a minimum set of data elements to report the extent of toxicities and their impact on treatment discontinuation. WHO also recommends complementing routine monitoring with active toxicity surveillance through specialized studies and surveys at sentinel sites to address specific concerns. Routine monitoring of ARV toxicity provides critical data on the incidence and clinical significance of severe toxicities, their impact on patient outcomes, and treatment retention. This information is vital for developing strategies to prevent and mitigate drug toxicity, thereby optimizing patient retention in care and improving treatment effectiveness. For the first time, a specific indicator for toxicity monitoring has been designated for national program monitoring. Disaggregating data by ART regimen, sex, age, pregnancy status, TB/HIV co-infection, and key populations (if available) provides additional insights into populations at higher risk for toxicity due to environmental, behavioral, or co-morbid factors, as well as the concurrent use of other medications. WHO emphasizes strengthening surveillance of key ARV toxicities at sentinel sites when additional data is needed to inform policy and improve treatment outcomes. Active surveillance for specific ARV toxicities within existing sentinel cohorts offers significant benefits, as these cohorts have reliable systems for capturing clinical and toxicity data. Focusing on one drug or the incidence of key toxicities enhances the accuracy of assessments. Surveillance during pregnancy and breastfeeding is particularly important. This includes prospective pregnancy-exposure registries to monitor toxicity in pregnant women and neonates, systems for assessing birth outcomes (e.g., stillbirths, preterm births, low birth weight, congenital anomalies, and early infant deaths), and prospective monitoring of mother-infant pairs for toxicity from birth through the breastfeeding period. WHO recommends routine monitoring of ARV toxicity during pregnancy and breastfeeding, focusing on three key areas: maternal adverse outcomes (e.g., treatment-limiting toxicities), adverse birth outcomes (e.g., stillbirths, preterm births, low birth weight, congenital anomalies, and early infant deaths), and adverse infant and child outcomes (e.g., health impacts on growth and development due to ARV exposure via breast milk). Adverse birth outcomes can be routinely monitored by integrating an additional indicator into the national M&E system. HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) is an emerging global concern as ART programs scale up. The development of HIVDR threatens the effectiveness of ART and the sustained reduction of HIV-related morbidity and mortality. WHO recommends integrating HIVDR prevention and assessment into every national HIV program. Routine monitoring of early warning indicators (EWIs) and periodic HIVDR surveys in specific populations are essential to inform ART regimen selection and the frequency of viral load monitoring. EWIs are quality-of-care indicators that alert clinic and program managers to conditions favoring virological failure and the emergence of population-level HIVDR. These indicators measure ART adherence, retention, and viral load suppression. WHO provides detailed guidance on conducting HIVDR surveys and recommends assessing pre-treatment HIVDR every three years in countries with generalized epidemics. Data from these surveys should support national decision-making, particularly when updating ART guidelines. Viral load (VL) suppression is a critical outcome indicator of HIV program performance and the best available measure of patient adherence to ART. WHO recommends scaling up VL monitoring, as it reflects the ability of facilities to provide care that prevents HIVDR. In well-performing ART programs, the majority of patients on ART are expected to achieve VL suppression. Where routine VL testing coverage is insufficient, population-level VL suppression can be estimated through surveys or modeling based on assumptions. National HIV care programs should review available VL data to monitor current levels of VL suppression among ART patients.
